chunks: Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya, from al-‘Amraki, from ‘Ali ibn Ja‘far, from his brother Musa ibn Ja‘far عليهما السلام, who said:

I asked him about the bedding of a Jew and a Christian upon which one sleeps. He said: “There is no harm, but one should not perform salat (prayer) in their clothes.” And he said: “A Muslim should not eat with a Magian from one bowl, nor seat him upon his bedding, nor his place of prayer, nor shake hands with him.” He said: And I asked him about a man who bought a garment from the market to wear, not knowing to whom it had belonged— is salat (prayer) valid in it? He said: “If he bought it from a Muslim, then let him perform salat (prayer) in it; and if he bought it from a Christian, then he should not perform salat (prayer) in it until he washes it.”

Al-Shaykh, may Allah the Exalted support him, said: The garment is also washed from the sweat of scavenging camels when it touches it, just as it is washed from other impurities. The following indicates that.

key_terms.الصَّلَاةُ: salat (prayer), whose validity is being asked about
key_terms.الْجَلَّالَةِ: an animal that feeds on filth, here referring to camels
key_terms.الْمَجُوسِيِّ: a Magian, mentioned here in rulings of social contact
key_terms.ثَوْبًا: a garment or item of clothing
key_terms.ثِيَابِهِمَا: the clothes belonging to the Jew and the Christian
key_terms.قَصْعَةٍ: a large bowl or dish used for shared eating
key_terms.مَسْجِدِهِ: his place of prostration or prayer spot

ai.seo_question: Can one pray in clothes bought from the market or used by a Christian or Jew?
ai.summary: This hadith presents legal rulings concerning ritual purity, interaction with certain non-Muslims, and the validity of salat (prayer) in garments of uncertain prior ownership. It distinguishes between items obtained from Muslims and Christians, and emphasizes washing in cases connected to najasah and suspected impurity.
